claim: Genetic drift is expected to remove polymorphism from populations over long periods of time.
source: Genetic drift is expected to remove polymorphism from populations over long periods of time, with the rate of polymorphism loss being accelerated when species experience strong reductions in population size.
evidence: This is a statement of established population genetics theory.

claim: The rate of polymorphism loss is accelerated when species experience strong reductions in population size.
source: Genetic drift is expected to remove polymorphism from populations over long periods of time, with the rate of polymorphism loss being accelerated when species experience strong reductions in population size.
evidence: This is a statement of established population genetics theory.

claim: Ancestral variation preferentially persists at immunity related loci in Capsella after species-wide bottlenecks.
source: We find that ancestral variation preferentially persists at immunity related loci, and that the same collection of alleles has been maintained in different lineages that have been separated for several million years.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by genomic analysis data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The same collection of alleles has been maintained in different Capsella lineages that have been separated for several million years.
source: We find that ancestral variation preferentially persists at immunity related loci, and that the same collection of alleles has been maintained in different lineages that have been separated for several million years.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by the identification of trans-specific SNPs across diverged lineages.

claim: Divergence between ancient haplotypes can be obscured by reference-based re-sequencing methods.
source: By reconstructing the evolution of the disease-related locus MLO2b, we find that divergence between ancient haplotypes can be obscured by referenced based re-sequencing methods, and that trans-specific alleles can encode substantially diverged protein sequences.
evidence: This is demonstrated through the MLO2b case study where de novo assembly revealed divergence not detected by reference-based mapping.

claim: Trans-specific alleles can encode substantially diverged protein sequences.
source: By reconstructing the evolution of the disease-related locus MLO2b, we find that divergence between ancient haplotypes can be obscured by referenced based re-sequencing methods, and that trans-specific alleles can encode substantially diverged protein sequences.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the MLO2b analysis showing 31 amino acid differences between haplogroups.

claim: Long-term balancing selection is an important factor shaping the genetics of immune systems in plants.
source: Our data point to long-term balancing selection as an important factor shaping the genetics of immune systems in plants and as the predominant driver of genomic variability after a population bottleneck.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the data showing enrichment of trans-specific polymorphisms at immunity loci.

claim: Long-term balancing selection is the predominant driver of genomic variability after a population bottleneck in Capsella.
source: Our data point to long-term balancing selection as an important factor shaping the genetics of immune systems in plants and as the predominant driver of genomic variability after a population bottleneck.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the observation that most retained variation after bottlenecks is at immunity loci.

claim: Balancing selection can have many causes, including heterozygous advantage, negative frequency-dependent selection, and environmental heterogeneity in space and time.
source: It can have many causes, including heterozygous advantage, negative frequency-dependent selection, and environmental heterogeneity in space and time.
evidence: This is a statement of established evolutionary theory.

claim: Balancing selection results in increased diversity at linked sites.
source: The unifying characteristic of these situations is that the turnover of alleles is slowed, resulting in increased diversity at linked sites (Charlesworth, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to established literature.

claim: Balanced alleles will be stochastically lost over long time spans.
source: However, balanced alleles will be stochastically lost over long time spans, suggesting that most balanced polymorphism is short lived (Fijarczyk and Babik, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Most balanced polymorphism is short lived.
source: However, balanced alleles will be stochastically lost over long time spans, suggesting that most balanced polymorphism is short lived (Fijarczyk and Babik, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: The strongest evidence for balancing selection comes from systems in which alleles are maintained in lineages that are reproductively isolated and that have separated millions of years ago.
source: The strongest evidence for balancing selection comes from systems in which alleles are maintained in lineages that are reproductively isolated and that have separated millions of years ago, resulting in trans-specific alleles with diagnostic trans-specific single nucleotide polymorphisms (tsSNPs).
evidence: This is a statement about the nature of evidence for balancing selection, supported by the examples that follow.

claim: Self-incompatibility loci of plants are targets of long-term balancing selection.
source: A few, well known genes fit this paradigm: the self-incompatibility loci of plants (Vekemans and Slatkin, 1994), mating-type loci of fungi (Wu et al., 1998), and the major histocompatibility complex (MHC) and ABO blood group loci in vertebrates (McConnell et al., 1988; Mayer et al., 1988; Lawlor et al., 1988; Watkins et al., 1990; Ségurel et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Mating-type loci of fungi are targets of long-term balancing selection.
source: A few, well known genes fit this paradigm: the self-incompatibility loci of plants (Vekemans and Slatkin, 1994), mating-type loci of fungi (Wu et al., 1998), and the major histocompatibility complex (MHC) and ABO blood group loci in vertebrates (McConnell et al., 1988; Mayer et al., 1988; Lawlor et al., 1988; Watkins et al., 1990; Ségurel et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: The major histocompatibility complex (MHC) in vertebrates is a target of long-term balancing selection.
source: A few, well known genes fit this paradigm: the self-incompatibility loci of plants (Vekemans and Slatkin, 1994), mating-type loci of fungi (Wu et al., 1998), and the major histocompatibility complex (MHC) and ABO blood group loci in vertebrates (McConnell et al., 1988; Mayer et al., 1988; Lawlor et al., 1988; Watkins et al., 1990; Ségurel et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: ABO blood group loci in vertebrates are targets of long-term balancing selection.
source: A few, well known genes fit this paradigm: the self-incompatibility loci of plants (Vekemans and Slatkin, 1994), mating-type loci of fungi (Wu et al., 1998), and the major histocompatibility complex (MHC) and ABO blood group loci in vertebrates (McConnell et al., 1988; Mayer et al., 1988; Lawlor et al., 1988; Watkins et al., 1990; Ségurel et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Six loci in primates have been identified as potential targets of long-term balancing selection and/or introgression.
source: These efforts have revealed six loci in primates (Leffler et al., 2013b; Teixeira et al., 2015) and up to 129 loci, that were identified by at least two shared SNPs each, in Arabidopsis (Novikova et al., 2016; Bechsgaard et al., 2017), as potential targets of long-term balancing selection and/or introgression.
evidence: This is supported by citation to published studies.

claim: Up to 129 loci in Arabidopsis have been identified as potential targets of long-term balancing selection and/or introgression.
source: These efforts have revealed six loci in primates (Leffler et al., 2013b; Teixeira et al., 2015) and up to 129 loci, that were identified by at least two shared SNPs each, in Arabidopsis (Novikova et al., 2016; Bechsgaard et al., 2017), as potential targets of long-term balancing selection and/or introgression.
evidence: This is supported by citation to published studies.

claim: Genes involved in host-pathogen interactions are enriched among candidate loci for balancing selection in both primates and Arabidopsis.
source: In both systems, genes involved in host–pathogen interactions were enriched, which in Arabidopsis is consistent with previous findings that several disease resistance loci appear to be under balancing selection in this species, based on the analysis of individual genes (Huard-Chauveau et al., 2013; Botella, 1998; Caicedo et al., 1999; Noel, 1999; Stahl et al., 1999; Tian et al., 2002; Bakker, 2006; Rose et al., 2004; Todesco et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple published studies.

claim: Several disease resistance loci in Arabidopsis appear to be under balancing selection.
source: In both systems, genes involved in host–pathogen interactions were enriched, which in Arabidopsis is consistent with previous findings that several disease resistance loci appear to be under balancing selection in this species, based on the analysis of individual genes (Huard-Chauveau et al., 2013; Botella, 1998; Caicedo et al., 1999; Noel, 1999; Stahl et al., 1999; Tian et al., 2002; Bakker, 2006; Rose et al., 2004; Todesco et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple published studies.

claim: The total number of examples with robust evidence for balancing selection across species in A. thaliana remains small.
source: However, even with the ability to conduct whole-genome scans for balancing selection in A. thaliana, the total number of examples with robust evidence across species remains small (Cao et al., 2011; 1001 Genomes Consortium, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published studies.

claim: Cases of long-term maintenance of alleles may be rare.
source: One explanation for this paucity of evidence for pervasive and stable balancing selection is that cases of long-term maintenance of alleles are rare.
evidence: This is presented as one possible explanation for limited evidence.

claim: Many studies lacked the power to detect the expected effects of balancing selection.
source: However, there are good reasons to believe that many studies lacked the power to detect the expected effects (Fijarczyk and Babik, 2015; DeGiorgio et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Self-fertilization greatly reduces the effective rate of recombination.
source: First, self fertilisation greatly reduces the effective rate of recombination, thus potentially expanding the footprint of balancing selection.
evidence: This is a statement of established population genetics theory.

claim: Self-fertilization potentially expands the footprint of balancing selection.
source: First, self fertilisation greatly reduces the effective rate of recombination, thus potentially expanding the footprint of balancing selection.
evidence: This is an inference based on the effect of reduced recombination.

claim: The transition to self-fertilization is generally associated with dramatic genome-wide reductions in polymorphism.
source: In addition, the transition to self fertilisation is generally associated with dramatic genome-wide reductions in polymorphism, potentially making it easier to detect outlier loci that retain variation from the outcrossing, more polymorphic ancestor.
evidence: This is a statement of established population genetics theory.

claim: Reduced polymorphism in selfers potentially makes it easier to detect outlier loci that retain variation.
source: In addition, the transition to self fertilisation is generally associated with dramatic genome-wide reductions in polymorphism, potentially making it easier to detect outlier loci that retain variation from the outcrossing, more polymorphic ancestor.
evidence: This is an inference about the statistical power to detect balancing selection.

claim: The ancestral state of Capsella is outcrossing, found in the extant diploid species C. grandiflora.
source: Like many plant lineages, the ancestral state of Capsella is outcrossing (found in the extant diploid species C. grandiflora), but selfing has evolved independently in two diploid species, C. rubella and C. orientalis (Figure 1A)(Foxe et al., 2009; Guo et al., 2009; Bachmann et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations and Figure 1A showing the phylogenetic relationships.

claim: Selfing has evolved independently in two diploid Capsella species, C. rubella and C. orientalis.
source: Like many plant lineages, the ancestral state of Capsella is outcrossing (found in the extant diploid species C. grandiflora), but selfing has evolved independently in two diploid species, C. rubella and C. orientalis (Figure 1A)(Foxe et al., 2009; Guo et al., 2009; Bachmann et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations and Figure 1A showing independent transitions to selfing.

claim: The genomes of C. rubella and C. orientalis exhibit drastic loss of genetic diversity typical for many selfers.
source: The genomes of both species exhibit the drastic loss of genetic diversity typical for many selfers (Figure 1B–C) (Guo et al., 2009; Foxe et al., 2009; St Onge et al., 2011; Slotte et al., 2013; Brandvain et al., 2013; Slotte et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations and Figure 1B-C showing the phenotypic differences.

claim: Loss of genetic diversity in C. rubella was initially thought to have occurred uniformly throughout the entire genome.
source: In the younger species, C. rubella, loss of genetic diversity was initially thought to have occurred uniformly throughout the entire genome (Foxe et al., 2009; Guo et al., 2009), but subsequent reports already hinted at some loci having increased diversity (Gos et al., 2012; Brandvain et al., 2013), motivating the present study.
evidence: This is supported by citations to earlier studies.

claim: Subsequent reports hinted at some loci having increased diversity in C. rubella.
source: In the younger species, C. rubella, loss of genetic diversity was initially thought to have occurred uniformly throughout the entire genome (Foxe et al., 2009; Guo et al., 2009), but subsequent reports already hinted at some loci having increased diversity (Gos et al., 2012; Brandvain et al., 2013), motivating the present study.
evidence: This is supported by citations to more recent studies.

claim: C. rubella is 30,000 to 200,000 years old.
source: The species Capsella rubella is young, only 30,000 to 200,000 years old, and was apparently founded when a small number of C. grandiflora individuals became self-compatible (Foxe et al., 2009; Guo et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: C. rubella was apparently founded when a small number of C. grandiflora individuals became self-compatible.
source: The species Capsella rubella is young, only 30,000 to 200,000 years old, and was apparently founded when a small number of C. grandiflora individuals became self-compatible (Foxe et al., 2009; Guo et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Previous studies hinted at unequal retention of C. grandiflora alleles across the C. rubella genome.
source: Previous studies had hinted at unequal retention of C. grandiflora alleles across the C. rubella genome (Gos et al., 2012; Brandvain et al., 2013), leading us to analyse this phenomenon systematically by comparing the genomes of 50 C. rubella and 13 C. grandiflora accessions from throughout each species' range (Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The study analyzed 50 C. rubella and 13 C. grandiflora accessions from throughout each species' range.
source: Previous studies had hinted at unequal retention of C. grandiflora alleles across the C. rubella genome (Gos et al., 2012; Brandvain et al., 2013), leading us to analyse this phenomenon systematically by comparing the genomes of 50 C. rubella and 13 C. grandiflora accessions from throughout each species' range (Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This describes the sample size and geographic distribution used in the study.

claim: 74% of the C. rubella reference genome remained accessible to base calling in both species after applying stringent filters.
source: Because the calling of trans-specific SNPs (tsSNPs) is particularly sensitive to mismapping errors in repetitive sequences, we applied a set of stringent filters, resulting in 74% of the C. rubella reference genome remaining accessible to base calling in both species, with almost half (47%) of the masked sites in the repeat rich pericentromeric regions.
evidence: This describes the filtering approach and its results.

claim: Almost half (47%) of the masked sites in the C. rubella genome are in the repeat rich pericentromeric regions.
source: Because the calling of trans-specific SNPs (tsSNPs) is particularly sensitive to mismapping errors in repetitive sequences, we applied a set of stringent filters, resulting in 74% of the C. rubella reference genome remaining accessible to base calling in both species, with almost half (47%) of the masked sites in the repeat rich pericentromeric regions.
evidence: This describes the distribution of masked sites.

claim: After filtering, there were 5,784,607 SNPs and 883,837 indels identified.
source: After filtering, there were 5,784,607 SNPs and 883,837 indels.
evidence: This reports the total number of variants identified.

claim: Only 27,852 SNPs were fixed between C. rubella and C. grandiflora.
source: Of these, only 27,852 were fixed between the two species, whereas 824,540 were found in both species (tsCgCrSNPs), consistent with the expected sharing of variation between the two species.
evidence: This reports the number of fixed differences between species.

claim: 824,540 SNPs were found in both C. rubella and C. grandiflora (tsCgCrSNPs).
source: Of these, only 27,852 were fixed between the two species, whereas 824,540 were found in both species (tsCgCrSNPs), consistent with the expected sharing of variation between the two species.
evidence: This reports the number of trans-specific SNPs.

claim: 4,291,959 SNPs segregated only in C. grandiflora (ssCgSNPs).
source: In addition, 4,291,959 SNPs segregated only in C. grandiflora (species-specific SNPs; ssCgSNPs), and 640,256 only in C. rubella (ssCrSNPs).
evidence: This reports the number of species-specific SNPs in C. grandiflora.

claim: 640,256 SNPs segregated only in C. rubella (ssCrSNPs).
source: In addition, 4,291,959 SNPs segregated only in C. grandiflora (species-specific SNPs; ssCgSNPs), and 640,256 only in C. rubella (ssCrSNPs).
evidence: This reports the number of species-specific SNPs in C. rubella.

claim: Sample rarefaction indicated that common ssCrSNP and tsCgCrSNP discovery was near saturation.
source: Sample rarefaction by subsampling our sequenced accessions indicated that common ssCrSNP and tsCgCrSNP discovery was near saturation in our experiment, though additional sampling will continue to uncover rare alleles (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by the rarefaction analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Additional sampling will continue to uncover rare alleles in Capsella.
source: Sample rarefaction by subsampling our sequenced accessions indicated that common ssCrSNP and tsCgCrSNP discovery was near saturation in our experiment, though additional sampling will continue to uncover rare alleles (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is an inference from the rarefaction analysis.

claim: C. rubella exhibits a dramatic reduction in genetic diversity consistent with a genetic bottleneck.
source: The consequences of selfing are easily seen as a dramatic reduction in genetic diversity in C. rubella (Figure 1—source data 2), consistent with the previously suggested genetic bottleneck (Foxe et al., 2009; Guo et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by the data and citations to previous studies.

claim: SNPs segregating in C. rubella were much less likely to be heterozygous than those segregating in C. grandiflora.
source: As expected from a predominantly selfing species, SNPs segregating in C. rubella were much less likely to be heterozygous than those segregating in C. grandiflora, though evidence for occasional outcrossing in C. rubella is observed in the form of a variable number of heterozygous calls (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Evidence for occasional outcrossing in C. rubella is observed in the form of a variable number of heterozygous calls.
source: As expected from a predominantly selfing species, SNPs segregating in C. rubella were much less likely to be heterozygous than those segregating in C. grandiflora, though evidence for occasional outcrossing in C. rubella is observed in the form of a variable number of heterozygous calls (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is an inference from the heterozygosity data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Linkage disequilibrium decayed to 0.1 within 5 kb in C. grandiflora.
source: Linkage disequilibrium (LD) decayed, on average, to 0.1 within 5 kb in C. grandiflora, while it only reached this value at distances greater than 20 kb in C. rubella (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by the LD decay analysis shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Linkage disequilibrium in C. rubella only reached 0.1 at distances greater than 20 kb.
source: Linkage disequilibrium (LD) decayed, on average, to 0.1 within 5 kb in C. grandiflora, while it only reached this value at distances greater than 20 kb in C. rubella (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by the LD decay analysis shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The best fit population structure model as determined by minimum cross-validation error was three clusters.
source: The best fit as determined by the minimum cross-validation error was three clusters, with one including all C. grandiflora individuals, and C. rubella samples split into two clusters.
evidence: This is based on ADMIXTURE analysis results.

claim: One cluster included all C. grandiflora individuals, and C. rubella samples split into two clusters.
source: The best fit as determined by the minimum cross-validation error was three clusters, with one including all C. grandiflora individuals, and C. rubella samples split into two clusters.
evidence: This describes the population structure results.

claim: PC1 separated the two Capsella species and PC2 separated the C. rubella samples.
source: Principal component (PC) analysis (Price et al., 2006) of genetic variation revealed a similar picture, with PC1 separating the two species and PC2 separating the C. rubella samples (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by the PCA results shown in Figure 2A.

claim: C. rubella population structure was strongly associated with geography.
source: C. rubella population structure was strongly associated with geography.
evidence: This is supported by the geographic distribution of genetic clusters.

claim: Samples from western Europe and southeastern Greece were unambiguously assigned to separate groups.
source: Samples from western Europe and southeastern Greece were unambiguously assigned to separate groups, while samples from northern and western Greece, near the presumed site of speciation in the current range of C. grandiflora (Hurka and Neuffer, 1997), showed mixed ancestry (or intermediate assignment to these groups, Figure 2A–B).
evidence: This describes the population structure results shown in Figure 2A-B.

claim: Samples from northern and western Greece showed mixed ancestry.
source: Samples from western Europe and southeastern Greece were unambiguously assigned to separate groups, while samples from northern and western Greece, near the presumed site of speciation in the current range of C. grandiflora (Hurka and Neuffer, 1997), showed mixed ancestry (or intermediate assignment to these groups, Figure 2A–B).
evidence: This describes the population structure results shown in Figure 2A-B.

claim: The general pattern of population structure is consistent with the centre of diversity for C. rubella being in northern Greece and a more recent rapid expansion into Western Europe.
source: The general pattern of population structure is consistent with the centre of diversity for C. rubella being in northern Greece and a more recent rapid expansion into Western Europe, and agrees with predictions made based on previous, smaller datasets (Brandvain et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an inference from the population structure data, supported by citation.

claim: One C. grandiflora sample was assigned partial ancestry to the otherwise C. rubella-specific clusters.
source: While a previous study had not found any evidence for such a scenario (Brandvain et al., 2013), one of our C. grandiflora samples was assigned partial ancestry to the otherwise C. rubella-specific clusters, and resided at an intermediate position along PC1 (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by the ADMIXTURE and PCA results shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Eastern C. rubella individuals were less differentiated from C. grandiflora compared to western C. rubella samples along PC1.
source: Furthermore, eastern C. rubella individuals, many of which grew in sympatry with C. grandiflora, were less differentiated from C. grandiflora compared to western C. rubella samples along PC1 (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C-D).
evidence: This is supported by the PCA results.

claim: Gene flow between eastern C. rubella and C. grandiflora was supported by significant genome-wide D-statistics.
source: Gene flow between eastern C. rubella and C. grandiflora was supported by significant genome-wide D-statistics for C. rubella samples from the C. grandiflora range (ABBA-BABA test; comparing each E individual with the W population) (Green et al., 2010; Durand et al., 2011), with D decreasing as a function of distance from the centre of C. grandiflora's range (Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by D-statistic analysis.

claim: D decreases as a function of distance from the centre of C. grandiflora's range.
source: Gene flow between eastern C. rubella and C. grandiflora was supported by significant genome-wide D-statistics for C. rubella samples from the C. grandiflora range (ABBA-BABA test; comparing each E individual with the W population) (Green et al., 2010; Durand et al., 2011), with D decreasing as a function of distance from the centre of C. grandiflora's range (Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by the D-statistic analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The proportion of the genome shared in IBD segments between C. rubella and C. grandiflora decreased as a function of distance between samples.
source: The proportion of the genome shared in IBD segments between C. rubella and C. grandiflora also decreased as a function of distance between samples, and the strongest evidence for recent ancestry was found between C. grandiflora individuals and sympatric northern Greek C. rubella lines (Figure 2C–D).
evidence: This is supported by IBD analysis shown in Figure 2C-D.

claim: The strongest evidence for recent ancestry was found between C. grandiflora individuals and sympatric northern Greek C. rubella lines.
source: The proportion of the genome shared in IBD segments between C. rubella and C. grandiflora also decreased as a function of distance between samples, and the strongest evidence for recent ancestry was found between C. grandiflora individuals and sympatric northern Greek C. rubella lines (Figure 2C–D).
evidence: This is supported by IBD analysis shown in Figure 2C-D.

claim: Gene flow is ongoing between C. rubella and C. grandiflora.
source: These results indicate that gene flow is ongoing between the species, consistent with interspecific crosses often producing fertile offspring, specifically with C. rubella as the paternal parent (Sicard et al., 2011; Rebernig et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an inference from the IBD and D-statistic data, supported by citations about hybrid fertility.

claim: Interspecific crosses between C. rubella and C. grandiflora often produce fertile offspring, specifically with C. rubella as the paternal parent.
source: These results indicate that gene flow is ongoing between the species, consistent with interspecific crosses often producing fertile offspring, specifically with C. rubella as the paternal parent (Sicard et al., 2011; Rebernig et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: The best fitting demographic model estimated the split between C. rubella and C. grandiflora to have occurred 170,000 generations ago.
source: The best fitting model estimated the split between C. rubella and C. grandiflora to have occurred 170,000 generations ago, associated with a strong reduction in C. rubella population size (to only 2–14 effective chromosomes, or 1–7 individuals).
evidence: This is based on demographic modeling using fastsimcoal2.

claim: The split between C. rubella and C. grandiflora was associated with a strong reduction in C. rubella population size to only 2–14 effective chromosomes, or 1–7 individuals.
source: The best fitting model estimated the split between C. rubella and C. grandiflora to have occurred 170,000 generations ago, associated with a strong reduction in C. rubella population size (to only 2–14 effective chromosomes, or 1–7 individuals).
evidence: This is based on demographic modeling using fastsimcoal2.

claim: Bidirectional gene flow occurred between C. rubella and C. grandiflora at a relatively low rate until just over 10,000 generations ago.
source: Bidirectional gene flow at a relatively low rate apparently occurred until just over 10,000 generations ago, when C. rubella split into the W and E populations, after which gene flow continued only from E C. rubella to C. grandiflora (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is based on demographic modeling shown in Figure 2E.

claim: C. rubella split into the W and E populations just over 10,000 generations ago.
source: Bidirectional gene flow at a relatively low rate apparently occurred until just over 10,000 generations ago, when C. rubella split into the W and E populations, after which gene flow continued only from E C. rubella to C. grandiflora (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is based on demographic modeling shown in Figure 2E.

claim: After the population split, gene flow continued only from E C. rubella to C. grandiflora.
source: Bidirectional gene flow at a relatively low rate apparently occurred until just over 10,000 generations ago, when C. rubella split into the W and E populations, after which gene flow continued only from E C. rubella to C. grandiflora (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is based on demographic modeling shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The close timing of the end of gene flow into C. rubella and the split into two populations suggests that westward expansion of the C. rubella range reduced the opportunity for gene flow from C. grandiflora.
source: The close timing of the end of gene flow into C. rubella and the split into two populations suggests that westward expansion of the C. rubella range reduced the opportunity for gene flow from C. grandiflora, with potential genetic reinforcement by the development of hybrid incompatibilities (Sicard et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an inference from the demographic modeling results.

claim: The population split and the end of introgression from C. grandiflora occurred around 13,500 years ago, assuming an average of 1.3 years per generation.
source: If we assume an average of 1.3 years per generation as found in the close relative, A. thaliana (Falahati-Anbaran et al., 2014), which has similar life history and ecology, the population split and the end of introgression from C. grandiflora occurred around 13,500 years ago.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the demographic model and an assumed generation time.

claim: The date of 13,500 years ago is similar to the spread of agriculture and the end of the last glaciation in Europe.
source: This date is similar to the spread of agriculture and the end of the last glaciation in Europe (Walker et al., 2009), suggesting that C. rubella's success might have been facilitated by one or both of these events.
evidence: This is an inference connecting the timing to known historical events, supported by citation.

claim: C. rubella's success might have been facilitated by the spread of agriculture and/or the end of the last glaciation in Europe.
source: This date is similar to the spread of agriculture and the end of the last glaciation in Europe (Walker et al., 2009), suggesting that C. rubella's success might have been facilitated by one or both of these events.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about factors contributing to C. rubella's expansion.

claim: Over half of the segregating variants in C. rubella were also found in C. grandiflora.
source: Yet, over half of the segregating variants in C. rubella were also found in C. grandiflora (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by the SNP discovery data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: tsCgCrSNPs are strongly enriched among high-frequency alleles in both Capsella species.
source: We found that tsCgCrSNPs are strongly enriched among high-frequency alleles in both Capsella species (Figure 3A, p-value << 0.0001 in C. grandiflora and C. rubella, Mann-Whitney U-test).
evidence: This is supported by the derived allele frequency analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: At allele frequencies greater than 0.25 in C. rubella, tsCgCrSNPs accounted for more than 80% of all variation.
source: At allele frequencies greater than 0.25 in C. rubella, tsCgCrSNPs accounted for more than 80% of all variation.
evidence: This is supported by the derived allele frequency analysis.

claim: tsCgCrSNPs are predominantly older alleles that were already present in the common ancestral population of C. rubella and C. grandiflora or that were introgressed from C. grandiflora to C. rubella prior to its expansion into western Europe.
source: These results indicate that tsCgCrSNPs are predominantly older alleles that were already present in the common ancestral population of C. rubella and C. grandiflora or that were introgressed from C. grandiflora to C. rubella prior to its expansion into western Europe.
evidence: This is an inference from the allele frequency data.

claim: The distribution of tsCgCrSNPs was uneven across the genome.
source: The distribution of tsCgCrSNPs was uneven across the genome.
evidence: This is supported by the genomic distribution analysis.

claim: When compared to ssCrSNPs drawn from the same allele frequency distribution, tsCgCrSNPs were less likely to result in nonsynonymous changes.
source: When compared to ssCrSNPs drawn from the same allele frequency distribution, tsCgCrSNPs were less likely to result in nonsynonymous changes (Figure 3B, p-value < 0.001, from 1000 jackknife resamples from the same allele frequency distribution), but they were more likely to be in genes (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by the annotation analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: tsCgCrSNPs were more likely to be in genes compared to ssCrSNPs.
source: When compared to ssCrSNPs drawn from the same allele frequency distribution, tsCgCrSNPs were less likely to result in nonsynonymous changes (Figure 3B, p-value < 0.001, from 1000 jackknife resamples from the same allele frequency distribution), but they were more likely to be in genes (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by the annotation analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Eighty-three percent of all tsCgCrSNPs were in complete LD with at least one other tsCgCrSNP in C. rubella.
source: As expected for transpecific haplotype sharing, eighty-three percent of all tsCgCrSNPs were in complete LD with at least one other tsCgCrSNP in C. rubella, and the density of tsSNPs along the genome was highly variable (Figure 3D–G).
evidence: This is supported by linkage disequilibrium analysis.

claim: The density of tsSNPs along the genome was highly variable.
source: As expected for transpecific haplotype sharing, eighty-three percent of all tsCgCrSNPs were in complete LD with at least one other tsCgCrSNP in C. rubella, and the density of tsSNPs along the genome was highly variable (Figure 3D–G).
evidence: This is supported by the genomic distribution shown in Figure 3D-G.

claim: tsCgCrSNP density was positively correlated with local genetic diversity in C. rubella.
source: tsCgCrSNP density was positively correlated with local genetic diversity in C. rubella (and less strongly so with genetic diversity in C. grandiflora; Figure 3F–I and Figure 3—figure supplements 2–5), and negatively correlated with differentiation between the species as measured by Fst (Figure 3J and Figure 3—figure supplements 2–5).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 3F-I.

claim: tsCgCrSNP density was negatively correlated with differentiation between the species as measured by Fst.
source: tsCgCrSNP density was positively correlated with local genetic diversity in C. rubella (and less strongly so with genetic diversity in C. grandiflora; Figure 3F–I and Figure 3—figure supplements 2–5), and negatively correlated with differentiation between the species as measured by Fst (Figure 3J and Figure 3—figure supplements 2–5).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 3J.

claim: The uneven pattern of diversity was similar in each C. rubella subpopulation.
source: The uneven pattern of diversity was similar in each C. rubella subpopulation (Figure 3—figure supplements 6–9), indicating that most of the retained polymorphism already segregated prior to colonisation.
evidence: This is supported by subpopulation-specific analyses.

claim: Most of the retained polymorphism in C. rubella already segregated prior to colonisation.
source: The uneven pattern of diversity was similar in each C. rubella subpopulation (Figure 3—figure supplements 6–9), indicating that most of the retained polymorphism already segregated prior to colonisation.
evidence: This is an inference from the similarity of diversity patterns across subpopulations.

claim: Most common genetic variation in C. rubella is also retained in its outcrossing ancestor C. grandiflora.
source: Thus, most common genetic variation in C. rubella is also retained in its outcrossing ancestor, and the rate of retention varies dramatically between genomic regions.
evidence: This is a summary inference from the trans-specific SNP data.

claim: The rate of retention of genetic variation varies dramatically between genomic regions in C. rubella.
source: Thus, most common genetic variation in C. rubella is also retained in its outcrossing ancestor, and the rate of retention varies dramatically between genomic regions.
evidence: This is supported by the uneven distribution of tsCgCrSNPs.

claim: tsCgCrSNPs were strongly biased towards genes involved in plant biotic interactions, including defense and immune responses.
source: We found that tsCgCrSNPs were strongly biased towards genes involved in plant biotic interactions, including defense and immune responses, and also toward pollen-pistil interactions, though less strongly (Supplementary file 1, Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by GO enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4A and Supplementary file 1.

claim: tsCgCrSNPs were biased toward pollen-pistil interactions, though less strongly than immune responses.
source: We found that tsCgCrSNPs were strongly biased towards genes involved in plant biotic interactions, including defense and immune responses, and also toward pollen-pistil interactions, though less strongly (Supplementary file 1, Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by GO enrichment analysis.

claim: Amongst the top ten enriched GO categories for biological processes were apoptotic process, defense response, innate immune response, programmed cell death, and defensive secondary metabolite production.
source: Amongst the top ten enriched Gene Ontology (GO) categories for biological processes were apoptotic process, defense response, innate immune response, programmed cell death, and defensive secondary metabolite production (specifically associated with terpenoids).
evidence: This is supported by GO enrichment analysis.

claim: 87% of genes annotated with apoptotic process were homologs of A. thaliana NLR genes.
source: Of genes annotated with apoptotic process, 87% were homologs of A. thaliana NLR genes, a class of genes best known for its involvement in perception and response to pathogen attack (Jones and Dangl, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by annotation analysis and citation.

claim: NLR genes are best known for involvement in perception and response to pathogen attack.
source: Of genes annotated with apoptotic process, 87% were homologs of A. thaliana NLR genes, a class of genes best known for its involvement in perception and response to pathogen attack (Jones and Dangl, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: tsCgCrSNPs falling in NLR genes were more likely than those in other types of genes to result in nonsynonymous changes.
source: An even higher enrichment for tsCgCrSNPs was found when testing this class of genes specifically, with tsCgCrSNPs falling in NLR genes being more likely than those in other types of genes to result in nonsynonymous changes (Figure 4A–B).
evidence: This is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 4A-B.

claim: Despite a severe global loss of genetic diversity, genes involved in plant-pathogen interactions have maintained high levels of genetic variation in C. rubella.
source: These results indicate that despite a severe global loss of genetic diversity, genes involved in plant-pathogen interactions have maintained high levels of genetic variation in C. rubella.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the enrichment of tsCgCrSNPs at immunity loci.

claim: tsCgCrSNPs and ssSNPs do not show evidence for increased heterozygosity that might indicate increased error rates in SNP calling.
source: That the distributions of these two metrics were nearly identical at tsCgCrSNPs and ssSNP sites indicates, however, that mismapping is unlikely to have affected our SNP calls (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the coverage and concordance analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: tsCgCrSNPs were not more likely to be found in the heterozygous state as compared to ssSNPs.
source: However, tsCgCrSNPs were not more likely to be found in the heterozygous state as compared to ssSNPs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the heterozygosity analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Elevated tsCgCrSNPs sharing and genetic diversity extended over 100 kb from NLR genes.
source: We found that elevated tsCgCrSNPs sharing and genetic diversity extended over 100 kb from NLR genes.
evidence: This is supported by the distance-based analysis of tsCgCrSNP density.

claim: Increased sharing of tsCgCrSNPs is not an artefact of the internal structure of NLR clusters.
source: Thus, increased sharing is not an artefact of the internal structure of NLR clusters (Figure 4B–C).
evidence: This is supported by the analysis excluding NLR clusters themselves, shown in Figure 4B-C.

claim: 21 genomic regions were identified as candidate targets of balancing selection (Bal regions).
source: After Bonferroni correction and joining of adjacent significant segments, we identified 21 genomic regions that we designated as candidate targets of balancing selection (Bal, Figure 4D and Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is based on Fst analysis compared to simulated neutral expectations.

claim: Bal regions showed substantially higher Tajima's D relative to the remainder of the genome.
source: Bal regions showed several classical indications of balancing selection including substantially higher Tajima's D and within-C. Rubella genetic diversity relative to the remainder of the genome (Figure 4E–F; p<<0.001 Mann-Whitney U-test for both statistics).
evidence: This is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 4E-F.

claim: Bal regions showed substantially higher within-C. rubella genetic diversity relative to the remainder of the genome.
source: Bal regions showed several classical indications of balancing selection including substantially higher Tajima's D and within-C. Rubella genetic diversity relative to the remainder of the genome (Figure 4E–F; p<<0.001 Mann-Whitney U-test for both statistics).
evidence: This is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 4E-F.

claim: tsCgCrSNPs in Bal regions were less likely to have been lost during colonisation of Western Europe than ssCrSNPs or tsCgCrSNPs in other parts of the genome.
source: tsCgCrSNPs in Bal regions were also less likely to have been lost during colonisation of Western Europe than ssCrSNPs or tsCgCrSNPs in other parts of the genome, and allele frequencies in Bal regions showed elevated correlation across populations (Figure 4—source data 2).
evidence: This is supported by the analysis of allele frequency changes during colonization.

claim: Allele frequencies in Bal regions showed elevated correlation across populations.
source: tsCgCrSNPs in Bal regions were also less likely to have been lost during colonisation of Western Europe than ssCrSNPs or tsCgCrSNPs in other parts of the genome, and allele frequencies in Bal regions showed elevated correlation across populations (Figure 4—source data 2).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis of allele frequencies.

claim: Bal regions did not show evidence for increased heterozygosity that might indicate increased error rates in SNP calling.
source: Like tsSNPs in general, Bal regions did not show evidence for increased heterozygosity that might indicate increased error rates in SNP calling (Median Observed - Expected Heterozygosity in 20 kb windows was −0.021 inside of Bal regions, and −0.020 outside of these regions).
evidence: This is supported by heterozygosity analysis.

claim: Nine of the 21 candidate Bal regions overlapped with clusters of NLR genes.
source: Of the 21 candidate regions, nine overlapped with clusters of NLR genes, and five with clusters of RLK/RLP or CRK genes, two classes of genes with broad roles in innate immunity (Yeh et al., 2015; Zipfel, 2008).
evidence: This describes the overlap between Bal regions and immunity gene clusters.

claim: Five of the 21 candidate Bal regions overlapped with clusters of RLK/RLP or CRK genes.
source: Of the 21 candidate regions, nine overlapped with clusters of NLR genes, and five with clusters of RLK/RLP or CRK genes, two classes of genes with broad roles in innate immunity (Yeh et al., 2015; Zipfel, 2008).
evidence: This describes the overlap between Bal regions and immunity gene clusters.

claim: RLK/RLP and CRK genes have broad roles in innate immunity.
source: Of the 21 candidate regions, nine overlapped with clusters of NLR genes, and five with clusters of RLK/RLP or CRK genes, two classes of genes with broad roles in innate immunity (Yeh et al., 2015; Zipfel, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Many of the specific Bal regions identified in Capsella have been directly demonstrated to function in disease resistance in A. thaliana.
source: Many of the specific regions we identified in Capsella have been directly demonstrated to function in disease resistance in A. thaliana (McDowell et al., 2000; McDowell, 1998; Goritschnig et al., 2012; Holub, 1994; Gassmann et al., 1999; Zhang et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2013; Xu, 2006; Yeh et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple published studies.

claim: RPP1 and RPP8 have been previously suggested as candidate targets of balancing selection.
source: RPP1 and RPP8 have been previously suggested as candidate targets of balancing selection, and trans-specific polymorphism has been reported at the RPP8 locus in the genus Arabidopsis (Bergelson et al., 2001; Wang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Trans-specific polymorphism has been reported at the RPP8 locus in the genus Arabidopsis.
source: RPP1 and RPP8 have been previously suggested as candidate targets of balancing selection, and trans-specific polymorphism has been reported at the RPP8 locus in the genus Arabidopsis (Bergelson et al., 2001; Wang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: The strongest signals of balancing selection are mostly derived from linked sites, rather than the clusters themselves.
source: Indeed the strong signal found in these regions could result from multiple linked balanced sites. Furthermore, the strongest signals of balancing selection are mostly derived from linked sites, rather than the clusters themselves, because confident SNP calling is very difficult, if not impossible, with short reads in the most complex genomic regions (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that NLR clusters are difficult to call SNPs in, shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Confident SNP calling is very difficult, if not impossible, with short reads in the most complex genomic regions.
source: Indeed the strong signal found in these regions could result from multiple linked balanced sites. Furthermore, the strongest signals of balancing selection are mostly derived from linked sites, rather than the clusters themselves, because confident SNP calling is very difficult, if not impossible, with short reads in the most complex genomic regions (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is a statement about the technical limitations of short-read sequencing.

claim: Genetic diversity was only modestly elevated in Bal regions in C. grandiflora.
source: Genetic diversity was only modestly elevated in these regions in C. grandiflora (p<<0.001 Mann-Whitney U-test, Figure 4E), and Tajima's D was not significantly different from other windows (Figure 4F), suggesting that this is not very likely.
evidence: This is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Tajima's D in Bal regions was not significantly different from other windows in C. grandiflora.
source: Genetic diversity was only modestly elevated in these regions in C. grandiflora (p<<0.001 Mann-Whitney U-test, Figure 4E), and Tajima's D was not significantly different from other windows (Figure 4F), suggesting that this is not very likely.
evidence: This is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Even in the case of elevated founder diversity, the observed Fst values in Bal regions remain exceptionally unlikely under neutral simulations.
source: We approximated this situation using our simulated genetic data. We subsetted simulations by the level of genetic diversity in C. grandiflora, choosing the top 1% of simulated values. Even in the case of elevated founder diversity in these data, the observed Fst values in Bal regions remain exceptionally unlikely (p<0.0001).
evidence: This is supported by simulation analysis.

claim: The observations point to ongoing balancing selection within C. rubella maintaining diversity in Bal regions.
source: These observations point to ongoing balancing selection within C. rubella maintaining diversity in Bal regions.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the Fst analysis and simulations.

claim: A larger fraction of Bal region sequence was found to be IBD when compared to the genome-wide average.
source: A larger fraction of Bal region sequence was found to be IBD when compared to the genome-wide average (Figure 4—figure supplement 2), consistent with elevated retention of introgressed alleles in these regions.
evidence: This is supported by IBD analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Shared IBD segments in Bal regions were on average shorter than those found in other parts of the genome.
source: Shared segments in Bal regions were on average shorter than those found in other parts of the genome, suggesting that they are older and have been subjected to longer periods of recombination since the introgression event (median within 3,503 bp, median outside 6,661 bp, Wilcoxon-rank sum test, p=1e-54), although we cannot exclude the influence of differing patterns of recombination in these regions as a contributing factor to this observation.
evidence: This is supported by IBD segment length analysis.

claim: Within the East population, IBD in Bal regions decayed as a function of distance from the C. grandiflora range in a manner comparable to the observed genome-wide pattern, albeit with a more shallow slope.
source: Within the East population, IBD decayed as a function of distance from the C. grandiflora range in a manner comparable to the observed genome-wide pattern, albeit with a more shallow slope (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by the geographic analysis of IBD shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: High levels of IBD were observed between C. grandiflora and West population accessions in Bal regions, in contrast to the genome-wide pattern.
source: In contrast to the genome-wide pattern, high levels of IBD were observed between C. grandiflora and West population accessions.
evidence: This is supported by IBD analysis.

claim: Allele sharing appears to be older in Bal regions and introgressed alleles have been retained for longer periods even after colonisation of Western Europe.
source: Thus, we find evidence for neutral gene flow throughout the genome, perhaps dominated by C. rubella to C. grandiflora introgression, as indicated by our demographic simulations. However, allele sharing appears to be older in Bal regions and introgressed alleles have been retained for longer periods even after colonisation of Western Europe.
evidence: This is an inference from the IBD patterns in Bal regions.

claim: Alleles were introgressed prior to the most recent range expansions in C. rubella, and variation was subsequently maintained by selection in Bal regions.
source: This latter observation is consistent with the hypothesis that alleles were introgressed prior to the most recent range expansions in C. rubella, and that variation was subsequently maintained by selection in Bal regions.
evidence: This is an inference from the IBD and allele frequency patterns.

claim: Selfing has evolved independently in C. orientalis, which diverged from C. grandiflora and C. rubella more than one million years ago.
source: The genus Capsella offers a unique opportunity to test the longevity of balancing selection, because selfing has evolved independently in C. orientalis, which diverged from C. grandiflora and C. rubella more than one million years ago and whose modern range no longer overlaps with the two other species, preventing ongoing introgression (Hurka et al., 2012; Douglas et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: The modern range of C. orientalis no longer overlaps with C. grandiflora and C. rubella, preventing ongoing introgression.
source: The genus Capsella offers a unique opportunity to test the longevity of balancing selection, because selfing has evolved independently in C. orientalis, which diverged from C. grandiflora and C. rubella more than one million years ago and whose modern range no longer overlaps with the two other species, preventing ongoing introgression (Hurka et al., 2012; Douglas et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: The study resequenced 16 C. orientalis genomes.
source: We therefore resequenced 16 C. orientalis genomes, to test whether there is evidence of balancing selection at similar types of loci.
evidence: This describes the sample size for C. orientalis.

claim: After alignment, SNP calling, and filtering, 71,454 segregating SNPs were identified in C. orientalis.
source: After alignment, SNP calling, and filtering, we identified a mere 71,454 segregating SNPs in C. orientalis.
evidence: This reports the number of SNPs identified in C. orientalis.

claim: C. orientalis shows an almost 50-fold reduction in diversity relative to the outcrossing C. grandiflora.
source: This is a surprisingly small amount of variation, corresponding to an almost 50-fold reduction in diversity relative to the outcrossing C. grandiflora (Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is based on comparison of diversity levels.

claim: C. orientalis diverged from C. grandiflora over 1.8 million generations ago.
source: Using our divergence and diversity measures, we estimated that C. orientalis diverged from C. grandiflora over 1.8 million generations ago (calculated as in ref. Brandvain et al., 2013).
evidence: This is based on divergence calculations.

claim: The probability of finding a single tsSNP between C. orientalis and C. grandiflora by chance is <4×10−19.
source: Using estimates of Ne from nucleotide diversity at four-fold degenerate sites (C. orientalis [14,643] and C. grandiflora [694,643]), the divergence time above, and the genome assembly size of 134.8 Mb, the probability of finding a single tsSNP is <4×10−19 using the methodology of Leffler and colleagues and Wiuf and colleagues (Leffler et al., 2013a; Wiuf et al., 2004), which assumes constant population size.
evidence: This is based on population genetics calculations using cited methods.

claim: 8,408 C. orientalis variants were shared with either C. rubella or C. grandiflora (ts2-waySNPs).
source: It was therefore surprising that 8,408 C. orientalis variants were shared with either C. rubella or C. grandiflora (ts2-waySNPs), and 3992 with both (ts3-waySNPs, Figure 5A–B).
evidence: This reports the number of two-way trans-specific SNPs.

claim: 3,992 C. orientalis variants were shared with both C. rubella and C. grandiflora (ts3-waySNPs).
source: It was therefore surprising that 8,408 C. orientalis variants were shared with either C. rubella or C. grandiflora (ts2-waySNPs), and 3992 with both (ts3-waySNPs, Figure 5A–B).
evidence: This reports the number of three-way trans-specific SNPs.

claim: In each of the three species, ts3-waySNPs were enriched at higher derived allele frequencies relative to ssSNPs and ts2-waySNPs.
source: In each of the three species, ts3-waySNPs were enriched at higher derived allele frequencies relative to ssSNPs and ts2-waySNPs, suggesting that they are on average the oldest SNPs (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by the derived allele frequency analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: 812 high quality transpecific SNPs segregating in all three Capsella species (ts3-wayhqSNPs) were identified.
source: We identified 812 high quality transpecific SNPs segregating in all three species (ts3-wayhqSNPs).
evidence: This reports the number of high-quality three-way trans-specific SNPs.

claim: The distributions of coverage and concordance values for ts3-waySNP sites were similar to other C. orientalis sites.
source: The distributions of coverage and concordance values in this dataset were similar between ts3-waySNP sites and other C. orientalis sites, further supporting their authenticity (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the quality control analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: In all three species, diversity was high directly adjacent to ts3-wayhqSNPs.
source: We examined diversity and divergence at neutral (four-fold degenerate) sites surrounding ts3-wayhqSNPs (Figure 5D). In all three species, diversity was high directly adjacent to ts3-wayhqSNPs, close to average levels for genome-wide divergence between the two Capsella lineages.
evidence: This is supported by the diversity analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The footprint of elevated diversity near ts3-wayhqSNPs is much more discernible in the two selfing species than in C. grandiflora.
source: This footprint of elevated diversity is much more discernible in the two selfing species than in C. grandiflora.
evidence: This is an observation from the diversity analysis.

claim: No obvious reduction in divergence was observed near ts3-wayhqSNPs.
source: No obvious reduction in divergence was observed near ts3-wayhqSNPs (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by the divergence analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: ts3-wayhqSNPs correspond predominantly to long-term maintained alleles that diverged on ancient time scales and are not the result of recent introgression.
source: We conclude that ts3-wayhqSNPs correspond predominantly to long-term maintained alleles that diverged on ancient time scales and that they are not the result of recent introgression.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the diversity and divergence patterns.

claim: The minor alleles at ts3-wayhqSNP sites are closer to intermediate frequencies in all three species compared to ts2-waySNPs.
source: In comparison to ts2-waySNPs, the minor alleles at ts3-wayhqSNP sites are closer to intermediate frequencies in all three species (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by the allele frequency analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: ts3-wayhqSNPs segregate at more similar allele frequencies in C. rubella and C. grandiflora than other two-way tsSNPs.
source: Furthermore, ts3-wayhqSNPs segregate at more similar allele frequencies in C. rubella and C. grandiflora than other two-way tsSNPs, as measured by Fst median values: 0.03 for ts3-wayhqSNPs and 0.16 for ts2-waySNPs, p<<0.001 Mann-Whitney test) and correlation of derived allele frequencies (Figure 4—source data 2).
evidence: This is supported by Fst and correlation analysis.

claim: The results suggest a conserved equilibrium maintained since the isolation of C. rubella and C. grandiflora over 10,000 generations ago.
source: These results suggest a conserved equilibrium maintained since the isolation of C. rubella and C. grandiflora over 10,000 generations ago.
evidence: This is an inference from the similar allele frequencies at ts3-wayhqSNPs.

claim: Derived allele frequencies for ts3-wayhqSNPs are not correlated between the two ancient Capsella lineages.
source: Derived allele frequencies for ts3-wayhqSNPs are not correlated between the two ancient Capsella lineages (Spearman's rho −0.08 C. orientalis to C. grandiflora and −0.04 to C. rubella).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis.

claim: It is possible that demographic reduction or habitat shift in C. orientalis has disturbed the equilibrium of allele frequencies.
source: It is possible that demographic reduction or habitat shift in C. orientalis has disturbed this equilibrium.
evidence: This is speculation about the cause of uncorrelated allele frequencies.

claim: ts3-waySNPs are strongly enriched in GO categories associated with immunity.
source: Like tsCgCrSNPs, ts3-waySNPs are strongly enriched in GO categories associated with immunity (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by GO enrichment analysis in Supplementary file 2.

claim: 50% of ts3-wayhqSNPs fell into the previously identified balanced regions.
source: Our previously identified balanced regions strongly predicted the genomic distribution of ts3-waySNPs; 50% of ts3-wayhqSNPs fell into these regions, even though they encompass fewer than 10% of tsCgCrSNPs and fewer than 3% of all SNPs, resulting in an even more skewed and uneven distribution of genetic diversity along the genome (Figure 5F–G).
evidence: This is supported by the overlap analysis shown in Figure 5F-G.

claim: At least one ts3-wayhqSNP was found in each of 10 of the 21 original candidate regions under balanced selection.
source: At least one ts3-wayhqSNP was found in each of 10 of the 21 original candidate regions under balanced selection.
evidence: This describes the overlap between ts3-wayhqSNPs and Bal regions.

claim: Six of the Bal regions with ts3-wayhqSNPs corresponded to NLR clusters.
source: Six of these corresponded to NLR clusters, two to RLK/RLP clusters, and one to a TIR-X cluster.
evidence: This describes the gene content of Bal regions with ts3-wayhqSNPs.

claim: Two of the Bal regions with ts3-wayhqSNPs corresponded to RLK/RLP clusters.
source: Six of these corresponded to NLR clusters, two to RLK/RLP clusters, and one to a TIR-X cluster.
evidence: This describes the gene content of Bal regions with ts3-wayhqSNPs.

claim: One of the Bal regions with ts3-wayhqSNPs corresponded to a TIR-X cluster.
source: Six of these corresponded to NLR clusters, two to RLK/RLP clusters, and one to a TIR-X cluster.
evidence: This describes the gene content of Bal regions with ts3-wayhqSNPs.

claim: There is very strong selection to maintain allelic diversity at specific immunity-related loci, even in a situation where a recent genetic bottleneck has wiped out almost all genetic diversity.
source: Thus, even in a situation where a recent genetic bottleneck has wiped out almost all genetic diversity, there is very strong selection to maintain allelic diversity at specific immunity-related loci, consistent with these alleles having persisted already for very long evolutionary times.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the C. orientalis data.

claim: The alleles at immunity-related loci are consistent with having persisted already for very long evolutionary times.
source: Thus, even in a situation where a recent genetic bottleneck has wiped out almost all genetic diversity, there is very strong selection to maintain allelic diversity at specific immunity-related loci, consistent with these alleles having persisted already for very long evolutionary times.
evidence: This is an inference from the presence of ts3-wayhqSNPs at immunity loci.

claim: A homolog of the A. thaliana MLO2 gene was selected for detailed analysis.
source: These filters singled out a homolog of the A. thaliana MLO2 gene as a particularly good candidate for more detailed analysis (Supplementary file 3 and Figure 6).
evidence: This describes the selection of MLO2 for case study analysis.

claim: MLO2 encodes a seven-transmembrane domain protein with a conserved role in plant disease susceptibility.
source: MLO2 encodes a seven-transmembrane domain protein with a conserved role in plant disease susceptibility (Figure 6A) (Consonni et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature and shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The C. rubella MLO2 locus has experienced a tandem duplication, resulting in two genes, MLO2a and MLO2b.
source: The C. rubella MLO2 locus has experienced a tandem duplication, resulting in two genes, MLO2a and MLO2b.
evidence: This describes the genomic structure at the MLO2 locus.

claim: All six ts3-wayhqSNPs at the MLO2 locus were in MLO2b.
source: Although both homologs are sufficiently diverged to be accessible to unambiguous read mapping, all six ts3-wayhqSNPs were in MLO2b (Figure 6B–C).
evidence: This describes the location of trans-specific SNPs at the MLO2 locus.

claim: In C. rubella and C. orientalis, the ts3-wayhqSNPs at MLO2b were arranged in five different haplotypes, which were collapsed into three related haplogroups, A, B and C.
source: In C. rubella and C. orientalis, the ts3-wayhqSNPs were arranged in five different haplotypes, which we collapsed into three related haplogroups, A, B and C (Figure 6B).
evidence: This describes the haplotype structure at MLO2b shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Haplogroup B in both C. rubella and C. orientalis exhibited similar patterns of low read coverage at the 5' end of MLO2b.
source: We found that haplogroup B in both C. rubella and C. orientalis exhibited similar patterns of low read coverage at the 5' end of MLO2b, suggesting a possible indel (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by the coverage analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The pattern of low coverage observed for haplogroup B at MLO2b was not due to structural variation, but instead to extremely high divergence from the reference haplogroup A.
source: Surprisingly, a comparison of the different haplotypes revealed that the pattern of low coverage observed for haplogroup B was not due to structural variation, but instead to extremely high divergence from the reference haplogroup A (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the de novo assembly analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Divergence between alleles within species at MLO2b was greater than 0.15 differences per bp.
source: Divergence between alleles within species was greater than 0.15 differences per bp, over three times higher than the genome-wide divergence between the species (Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by the divergence analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Divergence between MLO2b alleles within species was over three times higher than the genome-wide divergence between the species.
source: Divergence between alleles within species was greater than 0.15 differences per bp, over three times higher than the genome-wide divergence between the species (Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of within-locus and genome-wide divergence.

claim: De novo assembly allowed identification of a total of 204 additional tsSNPs at MLO2b, nearly all of which mapped to the 5' end.
source: De novo assembly allowed us to identify a total of 204 additional tsSNPs, nearly all of which mapped to the 5' end of MLO2b (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the de novo assembly results shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Neighbour-joining trees revealed the expected clustering of samples by species in regions adjacent to MLO2b, but clear clustering by haplogroup within the 5' region.
source: Neighbour-joining trees revealed the expected clustering of samples by species in regions adjacent to MLO2b, but clear clustering by haplogroup within the 5' region, a pattern that is reproduced in phylogenetic analysis of the entire CDS (Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by the phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Divergence within haplogroup across species at MLO2b was greater than, or similar to genome-wide averages for both A and B.
source: Importantly, divergence within haplogroup across species was greater than, or similar to genome-wide averages for both A and B, demonstrating that recent introgression did not give rise to allele sharing (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the divergence analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Recent introgression did not give rise to allele sharing at MLO2b.
source: Importantly, divergence within haplogroup across species was greater than, or similar to genome-wide averages for both A and B, demonstrating that recent introgression did not give rise to allele sharing (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the divergence analysis.

claim: In a 157 amino acid stretch of MLO2b, 31 amino acid differences are found between haplogroups A and B in both species.
source: In a 157 amino acid stretch, 31 amino acid differences are found in both species (Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 3), with an indel polymorphism accounting for another seven amino acid differences.
evidence: This is supported by the protein alignment shown in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: An indel polymorphism at MLO2b accounts for another seven amino acid differences between haplogroups.
source: In a 157 amino acid stretch, 31 amino acid differences are found in both species (Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 3), with an indel polymorphism accounting for another seven amino acid differences.
evidence: This is supported by the protein alignment.

claim: It seems likely that the two MLO2b haplogroups differ functionally.
source: The large number of differences between the two haplogroups makes it difficult to point to any specific change as the target of balancing selection, but it seems likely that the two alleles differ functionally, perhaps reinforced by additional differences in the promoter.
evidence: This is an inference from the large number of amino acid differences.

claim: The nucleotide divergence at MLO2b suggests that the haplogroups are much older than the split between the two species.
source: In summary, the nucleotide divergence in this region suggests that the MLO2b haplogroups are much older than the split between the two species.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the divergence analysis.

claim: Balancing selection plays a similar role in other taxa, but its effects are masked by a background of higher neutral genetic diversity and more frequent recombination.
source: We expect that balancing selection plays a similar role in other taxa, but that its effects are masked by a background of higher neutral genetic diversity and more frequent recombination between balanced sites and linked variants (Wiuf et al., 2004; Charlesworth, 2006).
evidence: This is speculation about the generality of the findings, supported by citations.

claim: The detection of long-term balancing selection is further compounded by very old alleles being less accessible to short read re-sequencing.
source: In addition, the detection of long-term balancing selection is further compounded by very old alleles being less accessible to short read re-sequencing, the dominant mode of variant discovery today.
evidence: This is a statement about technical limitations demonstrated by the MLO2b case study.

claim: In the two selfing Capsella species, the footprints of balancing selection extend for tens of kilobases.
source: In the two selfing Capsella species, the footprints of balancing selection extend for tens of kilobases, greatly impacting diversity of many other genes.
evidence: This is supported by the analysis of diversity around balanced sites.

claim: Extended LD in selfing species improves statistical power to detect causal regions of the genome but reduces the ability to identify the specific causal variants.
source: This is reminiscent of genome-wide association studies, where extended LD improves statistical power to detect causal regions of the genome but reduces the ability to identify the specific causal variants (Atwell et al., 2010).
evidence: This is an analogy to GWAS, supported by citation.

claim: Stable balancing selection in self fertilising species is unlikely to derive from heterozygous advantage.
source: Stable balancing selection in self fertilising species is unlikely to derive from heterozygous advantage, pointing to negative frequency-dependent selection or fluctuating selection from variable pathogen pressures as possible factors.
evidence: This is an inference based on the biology of selfing species.

claim: The strong signal of balancing selection observed in highly selfing lineages points to environmental heterogeneity or negative frequency dependent selection over heterozygote advantage.
source: While the mode of selection cannot be determined from these static data, the strong signal that we observe in highly selfing lineages points to environmental heterogeneity or negative frequency dependent selection over heterozygote advantage.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation of balancing selection in selfers.

claim: Based on the enrichment of immunity-related genes, it appears that biotic factors are the dominant drivers of long-term maintenance of polymorphism.
source: Based on the enrichment of immunity-related genes, it appears that biotic factors are the dominant drivers of long-term maintenance of polymorphism.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the GO enrichment analysis.

claim: This observation is consistent with a large body of work on intraspecific variation in A. thaliana.
source: This observation is consistent with a large body of work on intraspecific variation in A. thaliana.
evidence: This is a statement about consistency with prior literature.

claim: The signal of balancing selection has been observed for specific pairs of disease resistance alleles in A. thaliana.
source: The signal of balancing selection has been observed for specific pairs of disease resistance alleles in A. thaliana (Stahl et al., 1999; Tian et al., 2002; Tian et al., 2003; Mauricio et al., 2003; Bakker, 2006), and in the case of the resistance gene RPS5, alternative alleles have been shown to affect fitness in the field (Karasov et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Alternative alleles of the resistance gene RPS5 have been shown to affect fitness in the field.
source: The signal of balancing selection has been observed for specific pairs of disease resistance alleles in A. thaliana (Stahl et al., 1999; Tian et al., 2002; Tian et al., 2003; Mauricio et al., 2003; Bakker, 2006), and in the case of the resistance gene RPS5, alternative alleles have been shown to affect fitness in the field (Karasov et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a published study.

claim: It is possible that the signal of balancing selection is amplified by the fact that immunity-related loci occur in clusters.
source: It is possible, or perhaps even likely, that the signal of balancing selection is amplified by the fact that immunity-related loci occur in clusters (Meyers, 2003) and that our strongest signal is the result of simultaneous selection on several genes in these regions in a situation analogous to the MHC in animals (Hedrick, 1998).
evidence: This is speculation about the cause of strong signals, supported by citations.

claim: It is possible that the clustering of disease resistance genes itself is a product of selection.
source: On the other hand, it is also possible that the clustering of disease resistance genes itself is a product of selection, if selection was more effective when acting on groups of genes (Charlesworth and Charlesworth, 1975), or if evolution under a balanced regime was deleterious at other types of loci.
evidence: This is speculation about the evolution of gene clustering, supported by citation.

claim: The findings suggest a model in which the success of self fertilising populations may be buoyed by gene flow from outcrossing relatives.
source: Our findings suggest a model in which the success of self fertilising populations may be buoyed by gene flow from outcrossing relatives in a situation analogous to evolutionary rescue strategies in conservation biology (Whiteley et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the findings, with citation to analogous concept.

claim: This model is a variation on the theme of adaptive introgressions, which have recently emerged as a major evolutionary force in a wide range of taxa.
source: This model is a variation on the theme of adaptive introgressions, which have recently emerged as a major evolutionary force in a wide range of taxa (Whitney et al., 2006; Castric et al., 2008; Pease et al., 2016; Dasmahapatra et al., 2012; Henning and Meyer, 2014; Hedrick, 2013; Huerta-Sánchez et al., 2014; Racimo et al., 2015; Castric et al., 2008; Pease et al., 2016; Dasmahapatra et al., 2012; Whitney et al., 2006; Huerta-Sánchez et al., 2014; Hedrick, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple published studies on adaptive introgression.

claim: Constant replenishment via adaptive introgression from an outcrossing relative counters the loss of diversity at immunity-related loci in selfers.
source: Constant replenishment via adaptive introgression from an outcrossing relative counters the loss of diversity at immunity-related loci, thereby preventing decreased fitness in competition with pathogens.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the findings.

claim: Maintenance of ancient variants is most easily detectable in a background of low variation.
source: Finally, we note that maintenance of ancient variants is most easily detectable in a background of low variation.
evidence: This is a statement about the detectability of balancing selection.

claim: Maintenance of ancient variants could potentially be used to rapidly identify loci with meaningful functional variation.
source: Therefore, it could potentially be used to rapidly identify loci with meaningful functional variation.
evidence: This is speculation about potential applications.

claim: Identification of useful immunity-related polymorphism with genomic data might be facilitated in otherwise homogeneous wild populations.
source: Typically, agricultural breeding panels seek to maximise surveyed diversity, but our results indicate that identification of useful immunity-related polymorphism with genomic data might be facilitated in otherwise homogeneous wild populations.
evidence: This is speculation about potential applications to breeding.
